claim: More than 300 cities including Amsterdam have joined the UNAIDS Fast-Track Cities initiative.
source: More than 300 cities including the city of Amsterdam in the Netherlands have joined the UNAIDS Fast-Track Cities initiative, committing to accelerate their HIV response and end the AIDS epidemic in cities by 2030.
evidence: The abstract directly states this fact about the number of cities in the initiative.

claim: Between 1 January 2014 and 1 May 2019, there were 846 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents.
source: Between 1 January 2014 and 1 May 2019, there were 846 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents, of whom 516 (61%) were estimated to have been infected in 2014–2018.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ATHENA cohort data.

claim: 516 (61%) of the 846 Amsterdam HIV diagnoses were estimated to have been infected in 2014–2018.
source: Between 1 January 2014 and 1 May 2019, there were 846 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents, of whom 516 (61%) were estimated to have been infected in 2014–2018.
evidence: This is derived from biomarker-based estimation of infection times.

claim: The rate of new Amsterdam diagnoses since 2014 (104 per 100,000) remained higher than the national rates excluding Amsterdam (24 per 100,000).
source: Yet, the rate of new Amsterdam diagnoses since 2014 (104 per 100,000) remained higher than the national rates excluding Amsterdam (24 per 100,000), and in this sense Amsterdam remains a HIV hotspot in the Netherlands.
evidence: This is a comparison of observed diagnosis rates.

claim: Amsterdam remains a HIV hotspot in the Netherlands.
source: Yet, the rate of new Amsterdam diagnoses since 2014 (104 per 100,000) remained higher than the national rates excluding Amsterdam (24 per 100,000), and in this sense Amsterdam remains a HIV hotspot in the Netherlands.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher diagnosis rate in Amsterdam compared to the rest of the Netherlands.

claim: An estimated 14% [12–16%] of infections in Amsterdam MSM in 2014–2018 remained undiagnosed by 1 May 2019.
source: An estimated 14% [12–16%] of infections in Amsterdan MSM in 2014–2018 remained undiagnosed by 1 May 2019, and 41% [35–48%] in Amsterdam heterosexuals, with variation by region of birth.
evidence: This is estimated from biomarker data and time-to-diagnosis modeling.

claim: An estimated 41% [35–48%] of infections in Amsterdam heterosexuals in 2014–2018 remained undiagnosed by 1 May 2019.
source: An estimated 14% [12–16%] of infections in Amsterdan MSM in 2014–2018 remained undiagnosed by 1 May 2019, and 41% [35–48%] in Amsterdam heterosexuals, with variation by region of birth.
evidence: This is estimated from biomarker data and time-to-diagnosis modeling.

claim: An estimated 67% [60–74%] of Amsterdam MSM infections in 2014–2018 had an Amsterdam resident as source.
source: An estimated 67% [60–74%] of Amsterdam MSM infections in 2014–2018 had an Amsterdam resident as source, and 56% [41–70%] in Amsterdam heterosexuals, with heterogeneity by region of birth.
evidence: This is estimated from phylogenetic analysis and branching process modeling.

claim: An estimated 56% [41–70%] of Amsterdam heterosexual infections in 2014–2018 had an Amsterdam resident as source.
source: An estimated 67% [60–74%] of Amsterdam MSM infections in 2014–2018 had an Amsterdam resident as source, and 56% [41–70%] in Amsterdam heterosexuals, with heterogeneity by region of birth.
evidence: This is estimated from phylogenetic analysis and branching process modeling.

claim: An estimated 43% [37–49%] of locally acquired infections were in foreign-born MSM.
source: Of the locally acquired infections, an estimated 43% [37–49%] were in foreign-born MSM, 41% [35–47%] in Dutch-born MSM, 10% [6–18%] in foreign-born heterosexuals, and 5% [2–9%] in Dutch-born heterosexuals.
evidence: This is derived from combining phylogenetic estimates with demographic data.

claim: An estimated 41% [35–47%] of locally acquired infections were in Dutch-born MSM.

evidence: This is derived from combining phylogenetic estimates with demographic data.

claim: An estimated 10% [6–18%] of locally acquired infections were in foreign-born heterosexuals.
source: Of the locally acquired infections, an estimated 43% [37–49%] were in foreign-born MSM, 41% [35–47%] in Dutch-born MSM, 10% [6–18%] in foreign-born heterosexuals, and 5% [2–9%] in Dutch-born heterosexuals.
evidence: This is derived from combining phylogenetic estimates with demographic data.

claim: An estimated 5% [2–9%] of locally acquired infections were in Dutch-born heterosexuals.

evidence: This is derived from combining phylogenetic estimates with demographic data.

claim: The majority of Amsterdam MSM infections in 2014–2018 originated in transmission chains that pre-existed by 2014.
source: We estimate the majority of Amsterdam MSM infections in 2014–2018 originated in transmission chains that pre-existed by 2014.
evidence: This is estimated from phylogenetic reconstruction and branching process modeling.

claim: HIV is concentrated in metropolitan areas.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is concentrated in metropolitan areas (Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to UNAIDS.

claim: As of March 2021 over 300 cities have joined the Fast-Track Cities initiative.
source: In response, as of March 2021 over 300 cities have joined the Fast-Track Cities initiative (www.fast-trackcities.org) by signing the Paris Declaration, committing to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030, by addressing disparities in access to basic health and social services, social justice and economic opportunities (UNAIDS, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with reference to the Fast-Track Cities website and UNAIDS.

claim: Amsterdam is the city with the greatest HIV burden nationally in the Netherlands.
source: In the Netherlands, Amsterdam is the city with the greatest HIV burden nationally, reflecting in part large communities of MSM and foreign-born individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about Amsterdam's HIV epidemiology.

claim: Amsterdam joined the UNAIDS Fast-Track Cities initiative on 1 December 2014.
source: Amsterdam has a long history of a collaborative HIV approach in combating the epidemic and joined the UNAIDS Fast-Track Cities initiative on 1 December 2014.
evidence: This is a specific historical fact about Amsterdam's participation.

claim: The HIV Transmission Elimination Amsterdam project (H-Team) was initiated in 2014.
source: City-level HIV responses were galvanised in the HIV Transmission Elimination Amsterdam project (H-Team) that same year (de Bree et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Bree et al., 2019.

claim: The H-Team fast-track response focused on outreach activities, encouraging repeat testing every 3–6 months to identify acute and early HIV infection, followed by immediate initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy (c-ART) in newly diagnosed patients, and roll-out of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PreP) in populations at increased risk of HIV infection.
source: The H-Team fast-track response, amongst others, focussed on outreach activities, encouraging repeat testing every 3–6 months to identify acute and early HIV infection, followed by immediate initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy (c-ART) in newly diagnosed patients, and roll-out of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PreP) in populations at increased risk of HIV infection (den Daas et al., 2018; Bartelsman et al., 2017; Hoornenborg et al., 2019; Dijkstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the H-Team interventions.

claim: The number of annual HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents has consistently declined from ~300 new city-level HIV diagnoses in 2010 to ~120 in 2018.
source: Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of annual HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents has consistently declined from ~300 new city-level HIV diagnoses in 2010 to ~120 in 2018, primarily in Dutch-born and foreign-born MSM.
evidence: This is an observation from surveillance data.

claim: The decline in HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam was primarily in Dutch-born and foreign-born MSM.
source: Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of annual HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam residents has consistently declined from ~300 new city-level HIV diagnoses in 2010 to ~120 in 2018, primarily in Dutch-born and foreign-born MSM.
evidence: This is an observation from surveillance data.

claim: Late diagnoses remain common in Amsterdam.
source: Late diagnoses remain common and are a particular concern in this effort, both for individual health and the risk that unnoticed transmission chains pose to public health.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Data were obtained from the prospective ATHENA cohort of all people living with HIV (PLHIV) in care in the Netherlands.
source: Data were obtained from the prospective ATHENA cohort of all people living with HIV (PLHIV) in care in the Netherlands, including patient demographics and longitudinal CD4, HIV viral load, viral sequence, and treatment data (see Appendix 1, Section 2) (Boender et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the data source with a citation.

claim: 2% of individuals opted out of participating in the ATHENA study.
source: Cohort data are near complete in the sense that 2% of individuals opted out of participating in the ATHENA study, and 5.2% of individuals who entered ATHENA were lost to follow-up (Boender et al., 2018; Sighem et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a reported statistic about the cohort with citations.

claim: 5.2% of individuals who entered ATHENA were lost to follow-up.
source: Cohort data are near complete in the sense that 2% of individuals opted out of participating in the ATHENA study, and 5.2% of individuals who entered ATHENA were lost to follow-up (Boender et al., 2018; Sighem et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a reported statistic about the cohort with citations.

claim: Diagnosed infections were geolocated to Amsterdam based on patients' postcode of residence at time of first registration in ATHENA or the most recent registration update.
source: We geolocated diagnosed infections to Amsterdam based on patients' postcode of residence at time of first registration in ATHENA or the most recent registration update, which includes PLHIV that changed residence to Amsterdam at a registration update (4%), PLHIV that changed residence to another Dutch municipality after first registration (4%), and PLHIV that were consistently resident in Amsterdam (92%).
evidence: This describes the methodology for geolocation.

claim: 4% of PLHIV changed residence to Amsterdam at a registration update.
source: We geolocated diagnosed infections to Amsterdam based on patients' postcode of residence at time of first registration in ATHENA or the most recent registration update, which includes PLHIV that changed residence to Amsterdam at a registration update (4%), PLHIV that changed residence to another Dutch municipality after first registration (4%), and PLHIV that were consistently resident in Amsterdam (92%).
evidence: This is a reported statistic from the cohort data.

claim: 4% of PLHIV changed residence to another Dutch municipality after first registration.
source: We geolocated diagnosed infections to Amsterdam based on patients' postcode of residence at time of first registration in ATHENA or the most recent registration update, which includes PLHIV that changed residence to Amsterdam at a registration update (4%), PLHIV that changed residence to another Dutch municipality after first registration (4%), and PLHIV that were consistently resident in Amsterdam (92%).
evidence: This is a reported statistic from the cohort data.

claim: 92% of PLHIV were consistently resident in Amsterdam.
source: We geolocated diagnosed infections to Amsterdam based on patients' postcode of residence at time of first registration in ATHENA or the most recent registration update, which includes PLHIV that changed residence to Amsterdam at a registration update (4%), PLHIV that changed residence to another Dutch municipality after first registration (4%), and PLHIV that were consistently resident in Amsterdam (92%).
evidence: This is a reported statistic from the cohort data.

claim: Time from infection to diagnosis was estimated for all HIV diagnosed patients using a Bayesian approach.
source: Using longitudinal viral load and CD4 count data and further demographic and clinical information, we estimated time from infection to diagnosis for all HIV diagnosed patients with a Bayesian approach (Pantazis et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the methodology with a citation.

claim: Data from the CASCADE collaboration on 19,788 observed HIV seroconverters were used to parameterize a bivariate normal linear model.
source: Briefly, data from the CASCADE collaboration on 19,788 observed HIV seroconverters were used to parameterize a bivariate normal linear model of the joint time evolution of HIV viral load and CD4 cell count decline since time of infection in the context of additional covariates (sex, region of origin, mode of infection, age at time of diagnosis).
evidence: This describes the data used for model parameterization.

claim: Amsterdam patients had an average of four viral load observations and six CD4 cell count observations per patient.
source: Then we used the trained model to estimate infection times from longitudinal biomarker data for Amsterdam patients, with an average of four viral load observations and six CD4 cell count observations per patient.
evidence: This is a reported statistic about the data.

claim: A total of 275 (33%) of the diagnoses in MSM and heterosexuals presented with a CD4 count below 350.
source: A total of 275 (33%) of the diagnoses in MSM and heterosexuals presented with a CD4 count below 350, with late presentation being higher among heterosexuals.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cohort data.

claim: Late presentation was higher among heterosexuals than MSM.
source: A total of 275 (33%) of the diagnoses in MSM and heterosexuals presented with a CD4 count below 350, with late presentation being higher among heterosexuals.
evidence: This is a comparison from the cohort data.

claim: All diagnosed patients had biomarker data available to estimate time to diagnosis.
source: All diagnosed patients had biomarker data available to estimate time to diagnosis, and 516 of 846 (61%) were estimated to have been infected between 2014 and 2018 based on the posterior median infection time estimate (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the completeness of the biomarker data.

claim: In the preceding 5-year period 2009–2013, there were 1436 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam.
source: In the preceding 5-year period 2009–2013, there were 1436 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam and a similar proportion of these presented late (567, 39%).

claim: 567 (39%) of the 1436 diagnoses in 2009-2013 presented late.
source: In the preceding 5-year period 2009–2013, there were 1436 HIV diagnoses in Amsterdam and a similar proportion of these presented late (567, 39%).

claim: There were 1128 diagnoses with estimated infection in 2009–2013.

claim: There was a substantial reduction in infections in 2014–2018 compared to 2009-2013.
source: There were 1128 diagnoses with estimated infection in 2009–2013, suggesting a substantial reduction in infections in 2014–2018.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing infection estimates across time periods.

source: A total of 190 (37%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in Dutch-born MSM, 256 (50%) in foreign-born MSM, 23 (4%) in Dutch-born men and women identifying as heterosexuals, and 47 (9%) in foreign-born heterosexuals.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cohort data.

claim: 256 (50%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in foreign-born MSM.
source: A total of 190 (37%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in Dutch-born MSM, 256 (50%) in foreign-born MSM, 23 (4%) in Dutch-born men and women identifying as heterosexuals, and 47 (9%) in foreign-born heterosexuals.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cohort data.

claim: 23 (4%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in Dutch-born heterosexuals.
source: A total of 190 (37%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in Dutch-born MSM, 256 (50%) in foreign-born MSM, 23 (4%) in Dutch-born men and women identifying as heterosexuals, and 47 (9%) in foreign-born heterosexuals.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cohort data.

claim: 47 (9%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in foreign-born heterosexuals.
source: A total of 190 (37%) Amsterdam diagnoses with estimated infection in 2014–2018 were in Dutch-born MSM, 256 (50%) in foreign-born MSM, 23 (4%) in Dutch-born men and women identifying as heterosexuals, and 47 (9%) in foreign-born heterosexuals.

claim: The large majority of Amsterdam diagnoses with infection dates between 2014 and 2018 were in foreign-born and Dutch-born MSM.
source: Thus, the large majority of Amsterdam diagnoses with infection dates between 2014 and 2018 were in foreign-born and Dutch-born MSM, and an important question that we address below is if these diagnoses also likely had an Amsterdam source.
evidence: This is inferred from the proportions reported.

claim: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates among individuals were 14 months longer in heterosexuals than in MSM.
source: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates among individuals were 14 months longer in heterosexuals than in MSM, 9 months longer in Dutch-born heterosexuals than Dutch-born MSM, and 19 months longer in foreign-born heterosexuals than foreign-born MSM (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is derived from the time-to-diagnosis estimation model.

claim: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates were 9 months longer in Dutch-born heterosexuals than Dutch-born MSM.
source: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates among individuals were 14 months longer in heterosexuals than in MSM, 9 months longer in Dutch-born heterosexuals than Dutch-born MSM, and 19 months longer in foreign-born heterosexuals than foreign-born MSM (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is derived from the time-to-diagnosis estimation model.

claim: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates were 19 months longer in foreign-born heterosexuals than foreign-born MSM.
source: The posterior median time-to-diagnosis estimates among individuals were 14 months longer in heterosexuals than in MSM, 9 months longer in Dutch-born heterosexuals than Dutch-born MSM, and 19 months longer in foreign-born heterosexuals than foreign-born MSM (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is derived from the time-to-diagnosis estimation model.

claim: Local estimates indicate that Amsterdam has surpassed the 95-95-95 targets, with an estimated 5% of all people in Amsterdam living with HIV that remained undiagnosed by the end of 2019.
source: Local estimates of the continuum of care indicate that Amsterdam has surpassed the 95-95-95 targets, with an estimated 5% of all people in Amsterdam living with HIV that remained undiagnosed by the end of 2019 (Sighem et al., 2020; UNAIDS, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sighem et al., 2020 and UNAIDS, 2019.

claim: The highest proportion of undiagnosed Amsterdam infections in 2014–2018 are in heterosexuals born in Sub-Saharan Africa, with 57% [47–67%].
source: The highest proportion of undiagnosed Amsterdam infections in 2014–2018 are in heterosexuals born in Sub-Saharan Africa, with 57% [47–67%].

claim: 341 individuals were of the major subtypes or recombinant forms that are circulating in Amsterdam (B, 01AE, 02AG, C, D, G, A1 and 06 cpx).

claim: 1829 distinct viral phylogenetic subgraphs were identified that comprised at least one diagnosed Amsterdam infection prior to 2014.
source: We identified across the major HIV-1 subtypes and circulating recombinant forms 1829 distinct viral phylogenetic subgraphs that comprised at least one diagnosed Amsterdam infection prior to 2014, which we refer to as the phylogenetically observed pre-existing transmission chains (Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 26).
evidence: This is derived from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There were 1253 pre-existing chains in MSM.
source: There were 1253 pre-existing chains in MSM, of which 949 (76%) had all members virally suppressed as of 2014, and of those 906 (95%) had no new member in 2014–2018.

source: The proportion of unsuppressed subgraphs in Amsterdam heterosexuals was indeed statistically significantly lower than in Amsterdam MSM, but not strongly so (p-value 0.02, one-sided chi-square test).
evidence: This is derived from statistical testing of the phylogenetic data.

claim: Transmission appears to have stopped since 2014 in almost all phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains that had all their observed members suppressed by 2014.
source: To summarise, transmission appears to have stopped since 2014 in almost all phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains that had all their observed members suppressed by 2014.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that suppressed chains rarely grew.

claim: 89 (7%) of the 1253 phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains in Amsterdam MSM had at least one new member diagnosed in 2014–2018.
source: Considering growth, 89 (7%) of the 1253 phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains in Amsterdam MSM had at least one new member diagnosed in 2014–2018, and 114 chains emerged (Table 2 and Figure 3).

claim: 114 chains emerged in Amsterdam MSM in 2014-2018.
source: Considering growth, 89 (7%) of the 1253 phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains in Amsterdam MSM had at least one new member diagnosed in 2014–2018, and 114 chains emerged (Table 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is derived from the phylogenetic analysis.

source: In Amsterdam heterosexuals, 15 (3%) of the 576 phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains had at least one new member diagnosed in 2014–2018, and 26 chains emerged.

claim: 26 chains emerged in Amsterdam heterosexuals in 2014-2018.
source: In Amsterdam heterosexuals, 15 (3%) of the 576 phylogenetically observed pre-existing chains had at least one new member diagnosed in 2014–2018, and 26 chains emerged.

claim: An estimated 172 [154-195] emerging chains exist in Amsterdam MSM.
source: We estimate that there are substantially more emerging chains in Amsterdam since 2014 than phylogenetically observed, 172 [154-195] in MSM and 58 [42-83] in heterosexuals, reflecting that emergent chains have a high probability to be entirely unobserved when growth is below the epidemic reproduction threshold of one (Table 2).
evidence: This is estimated from the branching process model.

claim: An estimated 58 [42-83] emerging chains exist in Amsterdam heterosexuals.

evidence: This is estimated from the branching process model.

claim: Emergent chains have a high probability to be entirely unobserved when growth is below the epidemic reproduction threshold of one.

source: In terms of proportions, an estimated 61% [55–67%] of the growing chains among Amsterdam MSM were emerging, and 69% [56–81%] of the growing chains among Amsterdam heterosexuals.

claim: An estimated 61% [45–77%] of the estimated infections among Amsterdam heterosexuals in 2014-2018 were in emerging chains.
